PLANT TISSUE AND ANIMAL TISSUE

Tissue

  • Tissue is a group of cells that work together to perform a specific function in the body.

Tissues: Plant Tissue and Animal Tissue

Importance of Tissues

  • It causes division of labor in multicellular organisms.
  • It decreases workload on individual cells.
  • The organization of tissues into organs and systems leads to improved body organization.
  • Basic unit of life → Cell
  • Group of cells → Tissue
  • Group of tissues → Organs
  • Group of organs → Organ System
  • Group of organ system → Organism

PLANT TISSUE

  • Plant tissues are of broadly classified into two types: Meristematic Tissue and Permanent Tissue.

Meristematic Tissue

  • These tissues are made up of cells that can divide continuously, helping in plant growth.

Characteristics:

  • Occurrence: Growing regions of plant (root, shoot, etc.).
  • Shape: Spherical, oval, or rectangular.
  • Cells are small and thin, with dense cytoplasm and large nuclei.
  • Intercellular spaces and vacuoles are absent.
  • They are active cells.
  • Cell wall is made up of cellulose.

Protoderm is a part of apical meristem found in root and shoot and gives rise to epidermis.

Permanent Tissue

  • These are non-dividing cells that have attained maturity and perform specific functions.
  • Through the process of differentiation, meristematic tissues convert into permanent tissues.

Characteristics:

  • Occurrence: Roots, stem, leaves, etc.
  • Shape: Round or oval or elongated, polygonal, or even irregular.
  • Cell wall is thin or thick with large central vacuoles.
  • Functions: Permanent tissues in plants perform a variety of essential functions, including support, storage, conduction, and protection.

Cambium: A thin formative layer between xylem and phloem of most vascular plants that gives rise to new cells and is responsible for secondary growth.

Types of Meristematic Tissue

TypeLocationFunction
Apical MeristemPresent at shoot apex and root apexIncreases length of root and shoot
Lateral MeristemBeneath the barkIncreases thickness of root and stem
Intercalary MeristemAt the base of leaves or internodes (grasses)Increase in length of leaves and internodes (E.g. Leaf blades)

Types of Permanent Tissue

  1. 1. Simple Permanent Tissue: These tissues are also known as homogenous tissues. They are made up of a single cell type, usually with the same origin, structure, and function.

Types:

(a) Parenchyma Tissue

  • Occurrence: Throughout the plant body, particularly in soft parts like the cortex and pith of roots and stems, leaf mesophyll, and within vascular bundles.
  • They are living cells.

Functions:

  • It acts as a food storage tissue. In some cases, it contains chlorophyll, thus called Chlorenchyma.
  • When loosely packed, intercellular spaces are present called Aerenchyma. Aerenchyma provides buoyancy to parts and helps them to float.

(b) Collenchyma Tissue

  • Occurrence: In leaf stalks, stem of dicots epidermis and the vascular bundle of dicot leaf.
  • Cells are living, elongated, irregularly thickened at corners.
  • There is very little intracellular space in-between the cells.

Functions:

  • They act as mechanical tissue and thus provide mechanical strength to plants.
  • They provides flexibility (allow bending of parts). E.g. Tendrils and stems of climbers.

(c) Sclerenchyma

  • Occurrence: In stems, around vascular bundles, in leaf veins, and in the hard coverings (E.g. Bark, husk of coconut).
  • These are dead tissues, very hard and rigid in texture.

PLANT TISSUE AND ANIMAL TISSUE

  • They provide toughness to the tissue.

Functions:

  • These provide mechanical support and rigidity to the plant.
  • Sclereids are responsible for hardness of seeds and the shell of walnut.

Protective Tissue (part of simple tissue)

  • Protective tissues in plants are specialized tissues that form the outermost layers of the plant body, serving to shield it from various external factors like mechanical damage, pathogens, and water loss.
  • In plants, protective tissues include the epidermis and cork.

(a) Epidermis

  • The outermost layer of cells covering plant organs.
  • Occurrence: Occurs in outermost layer of all the plant parts. E.g. leaves, flowers, stem and roots.

Functions:

  • It protects all parts of plants.
  • Plants of dry habitats have thicker epidermis.
  • Plants growing in desert have cuticle (waxy coverings). Layer of cutin is called cuticle. Cutin is a waxy material and water resistant. It also aids in protection against water loss, injury and invasion of fungi.
  • Epidermal cells of the roots forms hair like structure. Long hair like parts increase absorption on surface area of roots.
  • In leaves, epidermal cells form stomata that are guarded by Guard cells. Guard cells are kidney shaped structures that regulate gaseous exchange in plants.

(b) Cork

  • Cork cells form the external protective tissue of plants. These cells are dead and compactly arranged, with their walls coated in suberin.
  • Occurrence: Outer covering of stem and tree trunks.

Functions:

  • It provides protection to mature roots and shoots.
  • Suberin acts as a protective barrier for the plants. The suberin does not allow the water and gases to go outside of the cork cells.

Transpiration Vs Guttation

TranspirationGuttation
Loss of water vapourLoss of water droplets
Through stomata, cuticle and lenticelsThrough hydathodes (Present on leaf sides)
Leads to loss of turgidity (wilting)No effects on turgidity
Cools the plant bodyNo cooling of plant body
Happens at day timeHappens at night time
  1. 2. Complex Permanent Tissue: These tissues are made up of various cell types that work together as a unit to perform a specific function.

Types:

(a) Xylem (Conducts water → One-way conduction)

  • It transports water and nutrients from the roots to the leaves of the plant through transpiration pull.
  • It provides support to the plants.
  • It is composed of: Tracheids, vessels, xylem fiber, and xylem parenchyma. Only xylem parenchyma is a living tissue.

(b) Phloem (Conducts food → Two-way conduction)

  • It translocates the prepared food from the leaves to different parts of the plant.
  • It is composed of: Sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, and phloem fibre (provides rigidity and support). Only phloem fibre is a dead tissue.

PLANT TISSUE AND ANIMAL TISSUE

ANIMAL TISSUE

  • Animal tissues are groups of similar cells with specific functions working together to form body structures.
  • Animal tissues can be broadly classified into four main types: Epithelial, Muscular, Connective, and Nervous tissue.

Epithelial Tissue

  • Occurrence: Widespread throughout the body.

Characteristics:

  • It acts as covering or protective tissue in animal body.
  • Cells form continuous sheet and are tightly packed with no intercellular spaces.
  • All epithelial tissues are separated by others through basement membrane.
  • Function: It protects the body from injury or damage.
  • There are two types of epithelial tissues: Simple epithelial and Compound epithelial tissue.
  1. 1. Simple Epithelial Tissue
  • Occurrence: Lining for body cavities, ducts, and tubes.
  • Structure: It is composed of a single layer of cells.
  • Simple epithelial tissue is further divided into three types: Squamous, Cuboidal, and Columnar.

(a) Squamous Epithelial Tissue

  • Occurrence: Lines blood vessels, air sacs of the lungs (alveoli), and body cavities like the peritoneum.
  • Structure: Cells are extremely thin and flat with irregular shape.

Types of Squamous Epithelial Tissue:

  1. 1. Simple Squamous Epithelial Tissue
  • Occurrence: Mouth and oesophagus (food pipe).

Characteristics:

  • They are single layer of cells, flattened with irregular boundaries.
  • They form delicate lining.
  1. 2. Stratified Squamous Epithelial Tissue
  • Occurrence: Skin.

Characteristics:

  • Cells are arranged in layers.
  • Prevents wear and tear.

Specialised tissue for healing → Granulation Tissue.

(b) Cuboidal Epithelial Tissue

  • Occurrence: Salivary glands, sweat glands, thyroid glands, lining of kidney tubules.
  • Structure: Cells have cube-like structure (height and width of the cells are equal).

(c) Columnar Epithelial Tissue

  • Occurrence: Lining of intestine, stomach and gallbladder.
  • Structure: The cells are pillar like, tall, and wide in appearance. Their nuclei is located at the base.

Ciliated Epithelial Tissue

  • Occurrence: Respiratory tract, urinary tubules or kidney.
  • Structures: Cells are cuboidal/columnar in shape with hair-like projections on their free surface called "cilia", which facilitates movement (particularly movement of fluids).
  • Function: Movement of mucus, urine, etc. through rhythmic beating of cilia.

Muscular Tissue

Structure:

  • It is composed of muscle cells or muscle fibres.
  • Muscle fibres are elongated and large in size. Contractile proteins are present in the fibres (important for movement of body).
  • Function: Contraction and relaxation, responsible for body movement.
  • Muscular tissue is further divided into three types: Skeletal muscle, Smooth muscle, and Cardiac muscle.
  1. 1. Skeletal Muscle
  • Occurrence: Skeletal part of the body (containing bones).

Characteristics:

  • Muscle fibres are elongated, unbranched and cylindrical in shape.
  • They are fast in nature.
  • They are voluntary muscles.
  • Each cell is multinucleated (many nuclei) with striations (alternate, dark and light bands).
  • These cells are easily fatigue.
  • Function: They help in body movement and maintaining posture.
  1. 2. Smooth Muscle
  • Occurrence: In organs like intestine, uterus, blood vessels, stomach, bronchi, iris.

Characteristics:

  • The nucleus is located at the centre of each cell.
  • Cells are non-striated, spindle shaped/fusiform which are held together by cell junction.
  • Cells are unbrached, slow in growth and do not fatigue easily.
  • They are involuntary muscles (not under our control).
  • Function: Muscle peristalsis (a wave-like movement that propels food and other substances through the digestive tract).

PLANT TISSUE AND ANIMAL TISSUE

  1. 3. Cardiac Muscle
  • Occurrence: Heart.

Characteristics:

  • Cardiac muscle fibres are long, cylindrical in shape.
  • Each fibre is uninucleated and branched.
  • Striations are present.
  • Cardiac muscles do not fatigue.
  • They are involuntary muscles (not under our control).

Functions:

  • They perform contraction and relaxation in wall of heart.
  • They help to pump and distribute blood to the body.

Connective Tissue

  • Occurrence: Tendons, cartilage, adipose tissue, ligaments, dermis, etc.

Characteristics:

  • It connects various body parts.
  • The cells are embedded in an intracellular matrix, this matrix may be jelly (cartilage), fluid (blood), dense or rigid (bone).
  • It acts like a binding, supporting and packing material.
  • It prevents organ from getting displaced by body movements.
  • Connective tissue is further divided into two types: Areolar connective tissue and Adipose connective tissue.
  1. 1. Areolar Connective Tissue

Characteristics:

  • It is a type of loose connective tissue that provides support, protection, and cushioning for various structures in the body.
  • It's characterized by a loosely arranged network of fibers and cells within a semi-fluid matrix, making it flexible and adaptable.
  • It is broadly divided into: Loose connective tissue and Dense connective tissue.

(a) Loose Connective Tissue

  • Occurrence: Between skin and muscles, in space inside organs, in bone marrow.
  • Structure: It is characterized by a loose, gel-like matrix consisting of cells, fibers, and a ground substance.

(b) Dense Connective Tissue

  • Characteristics: It has a high proportion of fibers, primarily collagen.

Types:

  1. 1. Tendons
  • It is a fibrous tissue with great strength and limited flexibility.
  • It connects Muscle to Bones.
  1. 2. Ligaments
  • It has considerable strength despite containing a small amount of matrix.
  • It connects Bones to Bones.
  1. 2. Adipose Connective Tissue
  • Occurrence: Below the skin (individuals with more body fat have more adipose tissue), in between internal organs.
  • Structure: Cells are round, oval shaped. There is an aggregation of fat cells (adipocytes).

Functions:

  • It prevents body from mechanical shock.
  • It acts as an insulator.

E.g. Camel hump.

Skeletal Connective Tissue

  • Skeletal connective tissues are connective tissues with unique structures and functions beyond basic support and connection.
  • They are broadly classified as: Cartilage and Bones.
  1. 1. Cartilage
  • Occurrence: Ear pinna, nose tip, trachea, larynx, bone surfaces at joints.

Characteristics:

  • They are widely spaced out cells.
  • Matrix is gel-like and slightly elastic.
  • Cartilage is flexible in nature.
  • Function: It supports and provides flexibility of body.
  1. 2. Bones

Characteristics:

  • Bones are hard and rigid, strong, and non-flexible in nature.
  • Matrix of the bone is hard and composed of calcium and phosphorous compounds.

Functions:

  • It forms a network of framework that supports the body.
  • It provides shape to body and protects the vital organs like brain, lungs, etc.

(c) Fluid Connective Tissue

  • It connects different part of the body and maintains continuity.
  • They are broadly classified as: Blood and Lymph.

PLANT TISSUE AND ANIMAL TISSUE

  1. 1. Blood

Blood: Liquid (55%) → Plasma (92%: Water, 8%: Protein, Salt, Hormones) | Solid (45%) → RBC, WBC, Platelets

Liquid Part of Blood

Plasma

  • It is the yellow in color.
  • It consists of 92% water and 8% proteins, salt and hormones.
ProteinsFunction
Fibrinogen/HeparinAnticoagulants
GlobulinProvides defence
AlbuminTo maintain osmotic balance

When clotting proteins are removed from blood, the clear liquid that remains after is called Serum.

Solid Part of Blood

RBC (Red Blood Cells)/Erythrocytes

  • Normal range: 4.5 to 5.5 million per cubic millimeter.
  • Color: Red in color due to presence of heme (Fe) Heme has high affinity towards oxygen.
  • Shape: Biconcave, disc-shaped.
  • Lifespan and Formation: Bone marrow (at birth) having a lifespan of about 120 days.
  • Function: It transports oxygen to whole body.
  • Mature RBC's have no nucleus in them.
  • Graveyard of RBC: Spleen.

Study of Blood: Hematology

WBC (White Blood Cells)/Leukocytes

  • Normal range: 5000-8000 per cubic millimeter.
  • WBC's protects our body from infection (provides our body a defence mechanism).
  • Formed in: Bone marrow having life span of 13-20 days.
  • Shape: Round/Irregular in shape.
  • Types: Monocytes, Lymphocytes, Neutrophils, Basophils, Eosinophils.

Platelets/Thrombocytes

  • Normal range: 1,50,000-3,50,000 per cubic millimeter of blood.
  • Shape: Irregular shape.
  • Formed in: Bone marrow having life span of a 7-10 days.
  • Function: They are essential for preventing and stopping bleeding by forming coagulation.
  • Low platelet count leads to thrombocytopenia (happens in case of dengue) and a very high platelet count leads to called thrombocytosis.
  1. 2. Lymph

Structure:

  • It is a colorless fluid.
  • RBC and blood proteins are absent in lymph.
  • Lymph is similar to blood plasma → contains proteins, salt, glucose, and water.
  • It is slightly yellow in color.

Function:

  • Lymph plays a crucial role in maintaining bodily fluid balance and supporting the immune system.

Nervous Tissue

  • Neural tissue (or nervous tissue) is a specialized tissue found in the nervous system.
  • It is responsible for receiving stimuli, transmitting signals, and coordinating responses throughout the body.
  • Occurrence: Found in Brain, Spinal cord, Nerves.

Anatomy of a Neuron

  • A neuron is the basic structural and fundamental unit of the nervous system. It is specialized to transmit nerve impulses.
  • Neuron is the longest cell in the human body.

Parts of Neurons:

  1. 1. Cell Body (Soma)
  • It contains the nucleus and cytoplasm and controls the activities of the neuron.
  1. 2. Dendrites
  • Short, branched extensions from the cell body that receives signals from other neurons or sensory cells.
  • It carries impulses toward the cell body.
  1. 3. Axon
  • It carries nerve impulses away from the cell body to other neurons or

PLANT TISSUE AND ANIMAL TISSUE

effectors (muscles/glands)

  1. 4. Myelin Sheath
  • A fatty layer that covers the axon that insulates the axon and speeds up signal transmission.
  1. 5. Schwann Cells
  • They are glial cells that form the Myelin Sheath on Axons is outside the brain.
  1. 6. Axon Terminals (Synaptic knobs)
  • The end branches of the axon that contain neurotransmitters.
  • It helps transmit signals to the next neuron or effector cell across a synapse.

Transmission of Neuron Impulses

  • A stimulus is received by the dendrites.
  • An electrical impulse travels through the cell body and axon.
  • At the axon terminals, the impulse triggers the release of neurotransmitters.
  • Neurotransmitters cross the synapse and pass the signal to the next neuron or effector (like a muscle or gland).
  • This leads to a response.

How do neurons transmit impulses (send message to other cells)?

One neuron's axon transmit information to other neuron's dendrite. The gap between these two is called synapse.

Camillo Golgi: First created the illustration of neuron using his silver-staining technique (Black Reaction).
